title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather, name the seasons, and use the weather sentences typical of Arabic.
bekal: ask and answer what the weather is like
name the four seasons and what each is like
use *al-jaww* as the subject of a sentence

dialogs.title: حِوَار — اَلْجَوُّ الْيَوْمَ
dialogs.intro: A windy morning in the campus courtyard.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: بَرْدٌ شَدِيدٌ الْيَوْمَ! كَيْفَ الطَّقْسُ عِنْدَكُمْ؟
lines.id: It's freezing today! What's the weather like where you're from?
lines.literal: cold severe today! how the-weather at-your(pl.)?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: فِي إِنْدُونِيسِيَا اَلْجَوُّ حَارٌّ طُولَ السَّنَةِ.
lines.id: In Indonesia it's hot all year round.
lines.literal: in Indonesia the-air hot all-through the-year.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لَا. عِنْدَنَا فَصْلَانِ فَقَطْ: اَلْجَافُّ وَالْمُمْطِرُ.
lines.id: No. We only have two seasons: dry and rainy.
lines.literal: no. at-us two-seasons only: the-dry and the-rainy.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: How many degrees is it usually?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: baina sab'in wa 'ishriina wa thalaathiina darajah.
lines.literal: between seven and twenty and thirty degree.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: يَا سَلَام! هُنَا فِي الشِّتَاءِ تَصِلُ إِلَى عَشْرٍ.
lines.baca: yaa salaam! hunaa fish-shitaa'i taṣilu ilaa 'ashr.
lines.id: Wow! Here in winter it can drop to ten.
lines.literal: O peace! here in the-winter it-reaches to ten.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Does it rain a lot in Cairo?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: أَبَدًا تَقْرِيبًا. اَلْمَطَرُ نَادِرٌ جِدًّا هُنَا.
lines.baca: abadan taqriiban. al-maṭaru naadirun jiddan hunaa.
lines.id: Hardly ever. Rain is very rare here.
lines.literal: never almost. the-rain rare very here.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: اَلرَّبِيعُ. اَلْجَوُّ مُعْتَدِلٌ وَالْأَزْهَارُ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ.
lines.baca: ar-rabii'. al-jawwu mu'tadilun wal-az-haaru fii kulli makaan.
lines.id: Spring. The weather is mild and there are flowers everywhere.
lines.literal: the-spring. the-air mild and the-flowers in every place.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: أَتَمَنَّى أَنْ أَرَاهُ. سَأَبْقَى حَتَّى مَايُو.
lines.baca: atamannaa an araah. sa'abqaa hattaa Maayuu.
lines.id: I hope I get to see it. I'm staying until May.
lines.literal: I-hope that I-see-it. will-I-stay until May.

notes: **اَلْجَوّ and اَلطَّقْس both mean "weather".** اَلْجَوّ is a little broader ("air, atmosphere") and more common in conversation; اَلطَّقْس is more technical and used in forecasts. An opener that is always safe: كَيْفَ الْجَوُّ الْيَوْمَ؟

**بَرْدٌ شَدِيدٌ — a sentence with no clear subject.** Literally just "severe cold", and that is already a full sentence. Arabic often states the weather as a bare noun: حَرٌّ (heat), بَرْدٌ (cold), مَطَرٌ (rain).
**تُمْطِرُ has no doer.** "It rains" is expressed with a feminine verb and nobody doing it — just like the empty *it* in English *it rains*.

**Indonesia really has only two seasons, and it takes explaining.** فَصْلٌ جَافّ (the dry season) and فَصْلٌ مُمْطِر (the rainy season). Arabs are almost always surprised to hear it — so if you come from a place with unusual weather, that's a topic that always works.
**كَمْ دَرَجَةً — singular with fathah again.** Just like كَمْ غُرْفَةً in unit 12. The same rule turning up a third time is exactly how it sticks.
**يَا سَلَام is an exclamation of amazement.** Literally "O peace", used just like "wow!" Other exclamations: وَاللهِ ("I swear!"), يَا إِلٰهِي ("oh my God").
**سَأَبْقَى — the letter سَـ marks the future.** It attaches straight to the front of a present verb. A longer, more emphatic form: سَوْفَ أَبْقَى. Unit 17 takes this apart fully.

grammars.title: Talking about the weather
after: Notice that the weather is almost always a nominal sentence: **[اَلْجَوّ] + [description]**, with no verb. You've had this structure since unit 1 — only the vocabulary is new.

grammars.title: The four seasons
after: Season names always take اَلْ, and "in (season)" uses فِي: فِي الصَّيْفِ (in summer), فِي الشِّتَاءِ (in winter).
You know the word فَصْل from unit 5 as "class". It really means "a separated part" — so it can be a class, a season, a semester or a book chapter.

blocks.text: Notice again that شَمْس (sun) and أَرْض (earth) are **feminine** even without ة, while قَمَر (moon) is masculine. This is the pair most often used as a reminder that the ة rule has exceptions.

blocks.title: Why the weather is the best small talk
items: In the Arab world, as anywhere, the weather is a conversation opener that never fails: safe, impersonal, and there is always something to say. An opener that always works: اَلْجَوُّ جَمِيلٌ الْيَوْمَ، أَلَيْسَ كَذٰلِكَ؟
And since people are always curious about other climates, describing the weather back home will keep the conversation going on its own, without you having to plan the next sentence.

blocks.text: The Islamic (Hijri) months are used alongside the Western ones, and their names are the same across the Arab world: مُحَرَّم, صَفَر, رَبِيعٌ الْأَوَّلُ, رَبِيعٌ الثَّانِي, جُمَادَى الْأُولَى, جُمَادَى الْآخِرَةُ, رَجَب, شَعْبَان, رَمَضَان, شَوَّال, ذُو الْقَعْدَةِ, ذُو الْحِجَّةِ. Ramadan is the one you probably know already.

Fill in the blanks with the right word.
Describe the weather in your city through the year, in at least five sentences.

Which season do you like best, and why?

answers: كَيْفَ الْجَوُّ الْيَوْمَ؟ — اَلْجَوُّ حَارٌّ جِدًّا. — اَلسَّمَاءُ غَائِمَةٌ. — تُمْطِرُ كَثِيرًا هُنَا. — كَمِ الدَّرَجَةُ الْيَوْمَ؟ — فِي إِنْدُونِيسِيَا فَصْلَانِ فَقَطْ.
حَارّ — بَارِد — مُعْتَدِل — مُمْطِر / رَطْب — جَافّ

Example: عِنْدَنَا فَصْلَانِ: اَلْجَافُّ وَالْمُمْطِرُ — اَلْجَوُّ الْيَوْمَ حَارٌّ وَرَطْبٌ — أَكْثَرُ شَهْرٍ حَرًّا هُوَ أُكْتُوبِر — تُمْطِرُ كَثِيرًا فِي يَنَايِر — أُحِبُّ الْفَصْلَ الْمُمْطِرَ لِأَنَّ الْجَوَّ مُعْتَدِلٌ
